summary: An empty/unavailable challenge list is interpreted as 'all solved', so a failed initial poll ends the run instantly with an empty result set and no error.
detail: Termination test is `unsolved_set = poller.known_challenges - poller.known_solved; active_now = any(...); if not unsolved_set and not active_now and not deps.pending_spawns: break` (lines 297-301). `PlatformPoller._seed` swallows every exception from the first fetch (`except Exception as e: logger.warning("Initial poll error: %s", e)`, poller.py:55-56), and `TSecBenchmarkPlatform.fetch_all_challenges` returns `[]` for any non-fatal HTTP/parse failure while raising RuntimeError only for the deliberate fatal states 'already finished'/'task_not_found' (tsec_platform.py:122-131). So when the very first poll fails (bad/expired token, VPN down, transient 5xx) or the platform reports zero challenges at start, `known_challenges` is empty and the first loop iteration logs 'All challenges solved; scheduler exiting.', `run_scheduler` returns `{'results': {}, 'total_cost_usd': 0, ...}`, and `cli._run_coordinator` prints 'Final Results:' plus a zero-cost summary as if the benchmark completed. The adapter author's explicit intent ('must NOT be mistaken for zero challenges — surface them instead') is defeated at the scheduler level.
fix_hint: Require positive evidence of one successful poll before the termination check: set a `seen_challenges` flag only when `_seed`/`_poll_once` complete without exception (propagate the adapter's fatal-state RuntimeError instead of logging it away), and only break when a non-empty challenge set was observed at least once; otherwise exit/raise so the CLI reports failure.
evidence: Confirmed. coordinator_loop.py:297-301: `unsolved_set = poller.known_challenges - poller.known_solved; ... if not unsolved_set and not active_now and not deps.pending_spawns: break` - an empty initial set fires on the first iteration, logging 'All challenges solved; scheduler exiting.' (:300) and returning results {}/cost 0 (:328-332), which cli._run_coordinator prints as a normal 'Final Results'. poller.py:48-56 swallows every exception from the first fetch, and tsec_platform.py:124-131 returns [] on non-fatal failures (the deliberate fatal states at :122-123 also raise into _seed's except). The CLI preflight (cli.py:61-76) catches bad-token/finished-task at startup, but transient first-poll failures and a zero-challenge payload still end the run silently as a false success.

summary: Lock fails open on an empty parsed hostname, and do_raw_http's scheme-prepending silently re-targets '//host' and '/host' URLs to that host.
detail: `h = (host or "").strip().lower(); if not h or h in deps.allowed_hosts: return None` treats an empty hostname as allowed. `http_request("//10.0.3.9/x")` -> headless_solver.py:159 `urlparse("http:////10.0.3.9/x").hostname is None` -> host "" -> no block; then net_tools.py:46-47 `url = "http://" + url.lstrip("/")` rewrites the request to `http://10.0.3.9/x`, which httpx fetches — an off-scope request with no lock check at all. A relative-looking call such as `http_request("/admin")` becomes a request to `http://admin/` (another VPN name) instead of the intended target, so the failure is both a bypass and a silent re-targeting. Nothing else re-validates the URL after the tool's pre-check.
fix_hint: Reject an empty hostname in _target_lock_block (never allow `not h`), and in do_raw_http refuse URLs without an explicit host instead of stripping '/'-prefixes; normalize the URL once in the tool and pass both the parsed URL and its host to the fetch.
evidence: backend/agents/headless_solver.py:125-126: `h = (host or "").strip().lower()` / `if not h or h in deps.allowed_hosts: return None` — an empty/unparseable host is allowed (fail-open) even when allowed_hosts is configured (block-all only when the set is empty, line 115). The URL path: line 159 `host = urlparse(url if "://" in url else f"http://{url}").hostname or ""` is the single check (161-167), then `return await do_raw_http(...)`. net_tools.py:46-47 `url = "http://" + url.lstrip("/")`: urlparse("http:////10.0.3.9/x").hostname is None → check skipped → lstrip('/') rewrites it to "http://10.0.3.9/x" (chained lstrip even strips leading 'h' chars of relative inputs like 'http:...'); a relative URL "/admin" becomes "http://admin". Nothing re-validates after this transformation, so the lock is bypassable by the solver's own input, directly contradicting prompts.py:137-138.

summary: `--no-submit` dry-run is broken end-to-end: real flags are submitted while the coordinator logs "DRY RUN"
detail: The submit tool's dry-run guard `if ctx.deps.no_submit:` (line 226, mirrored in `_submit_final_output_candidate` at 509) reads `HeadlessDeps.no_submit` (backend/deps.py:35, default False), which is never set: `HeadlessDeps(...)` is constructed at lines 346-363 without `no_submit`, and `HeadlessSolver.__init__` has no such parameter. The CLI does thread the flag as far as the swarm (backend/cli.py:295; coordinator_core.py:118), and `ChallengeSwarm.no_submit` exists (backend/agents/swarm.py:81) — but that line is the only occurrence of `no_submit` in swarm.py: `_create_solver` (swarm.py:139-152) never passes it down and `try_submit_flag` (swarm.py:186) never checks it, so `submit_fn` hits the live platform. Meanwhile coordinator_core.py:128 records `"submit": "DRY RUN" if deps.no_submit else ...` into the results. Net: with `--no-submit`, both solver-side guards are dead code and real submissions are made — the opposite of the requested contract.
fix_hint: Thread `no_submit` from `ChallengeSwarm` into `HeadlessSolver.__init__` and set `HeadlessDeps(no_submit=...)` (or enforce it at the top of `ChallengeSwarm.try_submit_flag`, returning `(f'DRY RUN — would submit "{flag}"', False)`), and add a test asserting no platform call is made under `--no-submit`.
evidence: Confirmed. headless_solver.py:226 `if ctx.deps.no_submit:` (mirror at :509) reads HeadlessDeps.no_submit, which nothing ever sets: deps.py:35 `no_submit: bool = False`; the HeadlessDeps construction (headless_solver.py:346-363) passes no such field and HeadlessSolver.__init__ (317-332) has no parameter for it. swarm.py:81 `no_submit: bool = False` is the only occurrence of the identifier in swarm.py; _create_solver (138-152) never forwards it and try_submit_flag reaches `result = await self.platform.submit_flag(self.meta.name, flag)` (:245). coordinator_core.py:128 still records '"submit": "DRY RUN" if deps.no_submit else "confirmed by solver"', and README.md:161 documents --no-submit as a dry run. Both solver-side guards are dead code and real submissions occur.

summary: --no-submit dry-run is not wired to solvers: flags are submitted for real
detail: ChallengeSwarm.no_submit is set by every caller (coordinator_core.py:118, cli.py:289-296) but never used inside the class: _create_solver() (swarm.py:138-152) does not forward it, HeadlessSolver.__init__ has no no_submit parameter (headless_solver.py:318-333), and HeadlessDeps.no_submit therefore stays False (deps.py:35). The dry-run guards at headless_solver.py:226 and :509 never fire, and try_submit_flag posts to the platform at swarm.py:245. coordinator_core.py:128 even labels the recorded result 'DRY RUN'. A run advertised as no-submit sends real flags and consumes the platform's wrong-answer budget.
fix_hint: Thread it through: _create_solver -> HeadlessSolver(no_submit=self.no_submit) -> HeadlessDeps.no_submit; add a defence-in-depth early return in try_submit_flag when self.no_submit is set.
evidence: Confirmed - same root cause as the headless_solver.py:226 finding. swarm.py:81 `no_submit: bool = False` is never read anywhere in the file (grep: it is the only occurrence in swarm.py); callers set it (cli.py:295, coordinator_core.py:118) but `_create_solver` (:138-152) does not forward it and HeadlessSolver/HeadlessDeps never receive it (headless_solver.py:317-332, 346-363; deps.py:35 stays False). The :226/:509 guards never fire and swarm.py:245 posts real flags to the live platform.

summary: Non-definitive submit statuses ('unknown' infra errors) are counted as wrong guesses and can trip the swarm-wide circuit breaker
detail: After the platform call only 'already_solved' (swarm.py:249) and 'correct' (swarm.py:256) are special-cased; every other status falls through to the wrong-submission accounting at swarm.py:273-279, which increments _submit_count/_wrong_total and at _wrong_total >= SUBMIT_LOCK_WRONG_LIMIT (4, swarm.py:184) sets _submit_locked and cancels the entire swarm with reason 'circuit_breaker' (swarm.py:276-284). TSecBenchmarkPlatform.submit_flag returns SubmitResult('unknown', ...) for challenge-not-found (tsec_platform.py:188), invalid_state (tsec_platform.py:230) and any non-duplicate HTTPStatusError (tsec_platform.py:234) — i.e. transient platform/VPN errors are indistinguishable from guessed flags. Four such errors stand the swarm down exactly as if four flags had been guessed, and each affected flag stays burned in _submitted_flags.
fix_hint: Branch on all statuses explicitly: treat 'unknown'/infra errors as retryable (return an error display, do not touch _submit_count/_wrong_total/_last_submit_time, and discard the flag from _submitted_flags); only 'incorrect' may feed the circuit breaker.
evidence: Confirmed. swarm.py special-cases only 'already_solved' (:249) and 'correct' (:256); every other status falls through to :273-279, which increments _submit_count/_wrong_total and at >= 4 (:184, :276-284) sets _submit_locked and cancels the swarm with 'circuit_breaker'. TSecBenchmarkPlatform.submit_flag returns status 'unknown' for challenge-not-found (tsec_platform.py:187-191), invalid_state (:228-233) and any non-duplicate HTTPStatusError (:234), so four transient platform/infra errors stand the swarm down exactly like four guessed flags, and each affected flag stays burned in _submitted_flags.

summary: `get_event` catches `asyncio.CancelledError` and returns None, so cancelling the scheduler task is silently discarded and shutdown hangs.
detail: `try: return await asyncio.wait_for(self._event_queue.get(), timeout=timeout) except (TimeoutError, asyncio.CancelledError): return None` (lines 75-80). `run_event_loop` awaits this once per ~1s iteration (coordinator_loop.py:206), so an external cancellation almost always lands here and is swallowed; the `while True` then continues polling and spawning. Concretely, `run_web_scheduler` shuts down with `if not scheduler_task.done(): scheduler_task.cancel()` followed by `with contextlib.suppress(...): await scheduler_task` (web.py:277-281) — the await blocks indefinitely because the task never acknowledges the cancel, so closing the web console leaves the scheduler running with containers still being opened. Likewise the first Ctrl+C under `asyncio.run` cancels the main task and waits for it; since the cancellation is eaten, the interrupt appears to do nothing and only a second signal force-kills the process, skipping the clean-shutdown path at coordinator_loop.py:303-326.
fix_hint: Swallow only the timeout (`except TimeoutError: return None`) and let `asyncio.CancelledError` propagate; if callers need a non-raising variant, expose a separate method or a `stopped` flag rather than aliasing cancellation with timeout.
evidence: backend/poller.py:75-80: `async def get_event(...): try: return await asyncio.wait_for(self._event_queue.get(), timeout=timeout) / except (TimeoutError, asyncio.CancelledError): return None` — a CancelledError delivered while the scheduler task is parked on the dominant await (coordinator_loop.py:206 `evt = await poller.get_event(timeout=1.0)`) is swallowed and converted to a normal None return, so the `while True` loop keeps ticking and the outer handler at coordinator_loop.py:303 (`except (KeyboardInterrupt, asyncio.CancelledError)`) never sees it. backend/web.py:277-281: `if not scheduler_task.done(): scheduler_task.cancel()` then `with contextlib.suppress(asyncio.CancelledError, Exception): await scheduler_task` — the guard-await can never complete while the task keeps looping, so console shutdown blocks. Python 3.14 stdlib confirms: asyncio/timeouts.py __aexit__ converts to TimeoutError only when the timeout itself expired; an external Task.cancel propagates as CancelledError into the except clause and, once caught, the task is no longer cancelled (asyncio/tasks.py wait_for docstring: 'If the task suppresses the cancellation and returns a value instead, that value is returned').

summary: Target lock is bypassed by HTTP redirects: httpx follows 3xx to any host, and the lock is only checked on the initial URL.
detail: headless_solver.py:159-167 runs `_target_lock_block` once on the original URL, then calls `do_raw_http`, which builds `httpx.AsyncClient(verify=False, timeout=timeout, follow_redirects=True, trust_env=False)` (net_tools.py:58-63). There is no allowlist parameter on `do_raw_http` and no re-check of `resp.url`, so a `302 Location: http://10.0.3.9/` served by an in-scope target is fetched automatically; the transcript even prints the off-scope `URL: {resp.url}` (net_tools.py:68) only after the fact. This violates the code's own invariant ('the solver's own egress is always restricted to the hosts parsed from this task's connection_info', headless_solver.py:103-107) and the prompt promise at prompts.py:137-138 ('http_request, tcp_send ... to any other host are blocked'). It is also the exact drift scenario the fail-loud lock was added for (c-03 incident).
fix_hint: Set follow_redirects=False and implement the redirect loop explicitly in do_raw_http, re-running the host check (per-hop allowlist callback passed from the tool, or an httpx event hook that raises on a non-allowed request URL); return the transcript with a 'redirect blocked' note when a Location points off-scope.
evidence: backend/tools/net_tools.py:58-63: `httpx.AsyncClient(verify=False, timeout=timeout, follow_redirects=True, trust_env=False)` — redirects are followed to arbitrary hosts with no per-hop allowlist re-check, and line 68 echoes `f"URL: {resp.url}"` back (final URL only). do_raw_http/do_tcp_send have no allowlist parameter (signature at net_tools.py:33-39) and grep shows they are only called from headless_solver.py (41, 167, 190), where the host is validated once before the call (headless_solver.py:159-167). A redirect emitted by any in-scope target therefore silently reaches an out-of-scope host, violating the target lock the system prompt promises at prompts.py:137-138 ('A target lock is enforced: http_request, tcp_send, and run_python socket connections to any other host are blocked') and the c-03 safety invariant.

summary: `steps` is always 0 for every non-flag outcome, so `EARLY_EXIT_MIN_STEPS` never discriminates: every failed swarm is mislabeled a startup failure and given a full second attempt.
detail: `steps = result.step_count if result else 0` — but `result` comes from `_run_swarm_with_time_limit`, which returns `run_task.result()` from `ChallengeSwarm.run()`. That method drops all non-FLAG_FOUND solver results (`for task in done: ... if result and result.status == FLAG_FOUND: return result`, then `tasks = list(pending)`) and finally executes `return self.winner` (swarm.py:459-462), which is None whenever no model found a flag. Therefore every failure that is not the wall-clock timeout (all solvers gave up, submit circuit-breaker `cancel_with_reason('circuit_breaker')`, stall watchdog withdrawal, error exits) reaches line 134 with `result is None`, so `steps < EARLY_EXIT_MIN_STEPS` (line 135) is unconditionally true: a swarm that consumed its entire 30-minute budget is logged as 'Early exit after 0 steps ... (likely a transient startup problem)', pushed to the coordinator inbox as such, added to `early_retried`, and given a second full-length run — doubling cost/time per failed challenge while the constant at line 22 and the per-solver `SolverResult.step_count` are dead in this path.
fix_hint: Carry a real step count out of the swarm: return the best non-win `SolverResult` from `ChallengeSwarm.run()` (or store `max(step_count)` across solvers on the swarm), and compare that here; alternatively read `max(a['step_count'] for a in swarm.get_status()['agents'].values())` before deciding to retry.
evidence: backend/agents/coordinator_core.py:134 `steps = result.step_count if result else 0`, then 135 `if steps < EARLY_EXIT_MIN_STEPS ...`. `result` comes from `run_task.result()` (line 171-172) of ChallengeSwarm.run(). swarm.py:452-457 returns a result only in the FLAG_FOUND branch; otherwise swarm.py:461-462 `self.cancel_event.cancel_with_reason("swarm_complete") / return self.winner`, and `self.winner = result` is assigned only at swarm.py:341 inside the FLAG_FOUND branch. So every non-flag finish (stall/gave-up/circuit-breaker/error) yields None → steps is always 0 → the retry branch fires unconditionally, ignoring EARLY_EXIT_MIN_STEPS (line 22), while SolverResult.step_count is in fact populated (headless_solver.py:592 `step_count=self._step_count[0]`). The early-exit logic is effectively 'retry every failed swarm once', contradicting README.md:46's '<15 steps' (步数过少) contract.

summary: Capacity accounting has two disagreeing sources of truth, and `open_containers` entries are never revalidated, so one failed container close permanently burns a local slot.
detail: `_recover_challenge_environment` returns early with 'keeping it counted' whenever `release_challenge` yields False (lines 204-216), and nothing ever retries the release or reconciles the set — `deps.open_containers` is only added at line 106 and discarded at line 217. A transient close failure therefore permanently reduces capacity: `do_spawn_swarm` gates on `active_count = len(deps.open_containers) + len(deps.pending_spawns)` (lines 52-53), so with TSec's 3-container cap, three such failures make every later spawn return 'At capacity (...)' for the rest of the run, and even the ghost reap (lines 85-102, which can close any challenge not in `running|pending|{challenge}`) never removes the name from the set. In the opposite direction, `_auto_spawn_one` (lines 479-483) and `_auto_spawn_unsolved` (lines 523-527) count only `swarm_tasks` + `pending_spawns`, so the scheduler keeps selecting 'free' slots, receives a refusal string from `do_spawn_swarm`, logs it as `Auto-spawn X: At capacity ...` (line 504), and resets spawn_failures. The adapter also under-counts: `release_challenge` ignores `close_challenge`'s `{'closed': resp.get('closed', True)}` result (tsec_platform.py:398-400 with release at 307-322), so a 200 response with `closed: False` is reported as a successful release and the name is discarded from `open_containers` while the range is still live.
fix_hint: Make one accounting source of truth (derive the scheduler's slot math from `open_containers | pending_spawns` too), re-attempt release or reconcile against the platform's `container_status` before keeping an entry counted, have the ghost reaper discard the names it closed, and have `release_challenge` return False when the payload says `closed: False`.
evidence: backend/agents/coordinator_core.py:211-217: `if released is False: logger.warning('Container for %s may still occupy a platform slot; keeping it counted', ...); return` / `deps.open_containers.discard(challenge_name)` — on release failure the name stays counted forever; grep shows open_containers is only mutated at line 106 (add) and 217 (discard). The ghost-reap path (coordinator_core.py:85-102) closes platform-side but never reconciles this set, and the capacity gate `len(deps.open_containers) + len(deps.pending_spawns)` (lines 52-53) plus scheduler predicates (coordinator_loop.py:479-483, 523-527, which ignore open_containers) rely on it. tsec_platform.py:398-400 returns `{'closed': resp.get('closed', True)}` but release_challenge (307-322) ignores the dict and returns True on no-exception, so a `closed: False` answer is invisible. Three such failures wedge every later spawn at 'At capacity' for the rest of the run.

summary: `--benchmark-base-url` silently has no effect: the platform adapter prefers platform_url, whose default is always non-empty.
detail: `base = settings.platform_url or settings.benchmark_url` (backend/agents/coordinator_loop.py:145). platform_url has a non-empty default 'https://tsecbench.zc.tencent.com' (backend/config.py:12-15), so the fallback never triggers; the CLI flag --benchmark-base-url only assigns `settings.benchmark_url` (backend/cli.py:87, 152-153) while the startup banner still prints it as the connection target (backend/cli.py:182), so an operator who redirects the run to another host via that flag keeps hitting the old one. The token side is the same trap that happens to work: `settings.platform_token or settings.benchmark_token` (coordinator_loop.py:146) only falls through because platform_token defaults to ''. Note both PLATFORM_* and BENCHMARK_* aliases feed the same URL field (backend/config.py:14 and :60), which is why the env route works but the flag route cannot.
fix_hint: Unify on one field/flag pair, or make --benchmark-base-url/--benchmark-token write settings.platform_url/settings.platform_token (or apply them in _create_platform).
evidence: Claim matches the code. coordinator_loop.py:145 `base = settings.platform_url or settings.benchmark_url`, and platform_url has a non-empty default `"https://tsecbench.zc.tencent.com"` (config.py:12-15), so the fallback never fires. `--benchmark-base-url` writes only `settings.benchmark_url` (cli.py:152-153), which feeds the banner (cli.py:182) and the VPN check (cli.py:209) but not the platform adapter. The env route works only because `BENCHMARK_BASE_URL` is also an alias of platform_url (config.py:14 vs :60); the token side (`settings.platform_token or settings.benchmark_token`, coordinator_loop.py:146) works because platform_token defaults to '' (config.py:16-19).

summary: The scheduler subsystem has zero tests despite being pure mechanical logic where every rule above is a silent-behavior regression risk.
detail: There is no `tests/` directory and no `test_*.py`/`conftest.py` anywhere in the repo (verified by find excluding .venv/.git), while pyproject.toml declares pytest/pytest-asyncio dev deps and docs/upgrade-rounds.md schedules an 'R4 test base'. The uncovered logic is exactly the fragile part: the two divergent capacity predicates (coordinator_core.py:52-53 vs coordinator_loop.py:479-483, 523-527), the early-exit retry bookkeeping (coordinator_core.py:130-147, currently unreachable in its intended form because steps is always 0), the deadlock timer math (coordinator_loop.py:446-471), spawn-failure deferral (coordinator_loop.py:500-514), REPL `__bump__` parsing (coordinator_loop.py:405-425), poller sanity/cancellation (poller.py:75-117) and the termination condition (coordinator_loop.py:297-301).
fix_hint: Add pytest-asyncio unit tests with a stub `CompetitionPlatform` and stub swarm: (a) capacity refuses at max and counts deferred containers; (b) a no-result swarm that ran more than EARLY_EXIT_MIN_STEPS is deferred, not retried; (c) deadlock fires only when unsolved is a subset of deferred and never clears operator-stopped entries; (d) poller skips empty/partial snapshots and propagates cancellation; (e) malformed `__bump__` payloads never propagate; (f) a failing initial poll does not report 'all solved'.
evidence: No test files exist anywhere outside .venv/.git: `find . -name 'test_*.py' -o -name '*_test.py'` and a check for `tests/`/`conftest.py` return nothing, despite pyproject.toml:29-31 declaring `pytest>=9.0`, `pytest-asyncio>=1.3` dev deps, and docs/upgrade-rounds.md:30 listing the R4 deliverable '测试基座（全模块 pytest 套件）'. The cited fragile paths (concurrency-accounting comparisons at coordinator_core.py:52-53 vs coordinator_loop.py:479-483/523-527, step-based early-exit coordinator_core.py:130-147, deadlock detection coordinator_loop.py:446-471, spawn-failure counter 500-514, REPL __bump__ parsing 405-425, poller.get_event/poll-sanity poller.py:75-117, termination condition coordinator_loop.py:297-301) are all unprotected.

summary: Deadlock test compares raw `deferred_challenges` size to unsolved count, so stale/operator-stopped entries can fake a deadlock; auto-resume then silently clears operator `/kill` deferrals.
detail: `and len(deps.deferred_challenges) >= len(unsolved_set)` mixes universes: `deferred_challenges` is never pruned when a challenge is solved or vanishes (entries are removed only by `/resume` at line 369/373 or by the auto-resume `clear()` at line 461), so solved challenges keep inflating the left side. Example: `unsolved={A}`, `deferred_challenges={S, T}` where S/T are already solved, and A's first spawn attempt just raised (spawn_failures[A]==1, A not in deferred, `active`/`preparing` empty because `_auto_spawn_unsolved` already returned). `2 >= 1` is true, so lines 455-457 start the idle timer and after `auto_resume_idle_seconds` line 461 executes `deps.deferred_challenges.clear()`, wiping deliberate 'stopped by operator' entries written by `_handle_kill` (line 397) and 'time limit reached' deferrals even though nothing was stalled. The condition that matches the intended 'all unsolved are deferred' is set containment.
fix_hint: Use `unsolved_set <= deps.deferred_challenges.keys()`; prune deferred entries for challenges present in `known_solved`, and tag operator-initiated deferrals so the auto-resume `clear()` can preserve them (or make auto-resume re-enable only spawn-failure/time-limit reasons).
evidence: backend/agents/coordinator_loop.py:449 `and len(deps.deferred_challenges) >= len(unsolved_set)` — a count comparison, not containment: a stale deferred entry for an already-solved (or never-unsolved) challenge inflates the left side. Deferred entries are removed only at lines 369/373 (_handle_resume) and line 461 (`deps.deferred_challenges.clear()`); nothing prunes them when a challenge is solved (grep confirms). Lines 455-461 then `deps.deferred_challenges.clear()` and resume everything — wiping operator 'stopped by operator' deferrals (line 397) and time-limit deferrals, which is exactly what the count check was meant to protect.

summary: `spawn_failures` is reset by non-error refusals and never cleared on re-enable, so the 'defer after 2 consecutive failures' policy cannot work as written.
detail: `deps.spawn_failures.pop(challenge_name, None)` (line 503) executes after ANY normal return of `do_spawn_swarm`, including the refusal strings 'At capacity (...)', 'Swarm still running', 'Swarm is already being prepared', 'Challenge ... is deferred' and 'Challenge ... not found on platform' (coordinator_core.py:37-57, 76); only exceptions increment the counter (lines 509-513). The intended scenario in the comment (ghost containers cause capacity walls) alternates exactly like that: a `/start` failure raises (fails=1), the next tick returns a normal 'At capacity' refusal (counter reset to 0), so `fails >= 2` is never reached and the challenge is re-attempted every refill tick, each attempt paying a full `fetch_all_challenges` plus the `/start` retry loop. Conversely nothing clears the counter when the challenge is re-enabled: after deferral at fails==2, a later `/resume` (lines 373-386) or the auto-resume `clear()` gives the challenge exactly one attempt before it is re-deferred as 'spawn failed 3x'; the `/resume` branch also prints 'Re-enabled deferred challenge' unconditionally even when `_auto_spawn_one` immediately refuses for capacity or budget.
fix_hint: Distinguish 'spawned' from 'refused' (exception or a structured return), only pop the failure counter on a genuine spawn, and clear `deps.spawn_failures.pop(name, None)` inside `_handle_resume` and the auto-resume path; report the real spawn outcome in the operator message.
evidence: backend/agents/coordinator_loop.py:500-503: `result = await do_spawn_swarm(deps, challenge_name)` then `deps.spawn_failures.pop(challenge_name, None)` on ANY normal return — including the refusals 'At capacity ...' / 'Swarm still running for ...' / already-deferred / not-found (coordinator_core.py:37-57 and 76). Only the except branch (509-513) increments `deps.spawn_failures`, so one exception after a /resume immediately re-defers the challenge as 'spawn failed 3x', and /resume's log at line 386 prints 'Re-enabled' unconditionally without resetting or reporting the stale fail count.

summary: Zero tests exist in the repo; the scope boundary (_parse_allowed_hosts/_target_lock_block) has no coverage, and the IPv6 parse defect above would be caught by one table-driven test.

summary: `task_status` reports a frozen accepted-flag count, contradicting the prompt's ground-truth instruction and inviting duplicate resubmissions

So a genuinely accepted flag looks unaccepted, and the model is pushed to re-submit (which the swarm dedups into "INCORRECT — already tried this exact flag.") or to keep burning budget on a solved flag.

summary: Tokens consumed by an interrupted/failed run are never recorded; `_result`'s "usage event on EVERY exit" backstop emits nothing for a first-run failure
detail: `self.cost_tracker.record(...)` (line 459) runs only after `await self._agent.run(...)` returns normally. A run that raises (CancelledError, provider/network error) has its tokens thrown away: they never reach `cost_tracker` and never reach the trace, so cost totals and budget decisions under-report (exactly the case the comments at 564-566 claim to cover). The `_result` delta block (562-578) can only re-emit deltas of usage that was already recorded into `cost_tracker.by_agent`; when the first run fails, `agent_usage` is None (563) and no usage event is emitted at all, so "a usage event lands on EVERY exit" is false.

Tokens consumed by a cancelled/errored run are lost from both cost totals and the trace, contradicting the comment at :564-567 ('a usage event lands on EVERY exit').

summary: Rescue auto-submissions feed the swarm-wide wrong-flag circuit breaker and can cancel every sibling solver
detail: The rescue loop `for candidate in _extract_flag_candidates(output): await self._submit_final_output_candidate(candidate)` (475-478) submits every flag-shaped token in the model's closing prose through `submit_fn` -> `swarm.try_submit_flag`. Each incorrect one increments `self._wrong_total` (backend/agents/swarm.py:275) and at `SUBMIT_LOCK_WRONG_LIMIT = 4` (swarm.py:184) the whole swarm is killed via `cancel_event.cancel_with_reason("circuit_breaker")` (swarm.py:276-280). A chatty model whose final summary lists several decoys can, by itself, cancel every sibling solver on the task in a single step — and the model never knows these submissions happened, so it cannot correct course.
fix_hint: Limit rescue submissions (e.g. at most one candidate the model explicitly presented as the flag, or only when it differs from every rejected candidate), or exclude rescue-driven submissions from `_wrong_total` accounting.
evidence: Confirmed. headless_solver.py:475-478 submits every `_extract_flag_candidates(output)` through `_submit_final_output_candidate`, which calls `self.deps.submit_fn(candidate)` (:522-523) -> swarm.try_submit_flag; each non-correct result does `self._wrong_total += 1` (swarm.py:275) and at SUBMIT_LOCK_WRONG_LIMIT=4 (:184) `self.cancel_event.cancel_with_reason('circuit_breaker')` (:280) stands the whole swarm down. Rescue submissions/results are only appended to _findings and the tracer, never shown to the model, so several decoys in one closing summary can trip the breaker unaided.

summary: Confirmed flag is discarded on the generic Exception path — the CancelledError handler has the guard, the Exception handler does not
detail: The `except asyncio.CancelledError` handler (491-500) explicitly re-checks `self.deps.confirmed_flag and not self._confirmed` and returns FLAG_FOUND because "the run can be cancelled between the platform's flag confirmation and this return". The `except Exception as e:` handler (501-505) returns `self._result(ERROR)` with no such check. Any non-cancel exception raised after `submit_fn`/`do_submit_flag` confirmed the flag (e.g. a tracer write failure inside `_submit_final_output_candidate`, a submit-tool error surfacing during result processing, a network error in the same agent turn) makes the solver report ERROR, so the swarm and coordinator never record the solve even though the platform already accepted the flag.
fix_hint: Mirror the CancelledError guard in the Exception handler, or centralize the check inside `_result`: if `deps.confirmed_flag` is set, FLAG_FOUND wins over ERROR.
evidence: Confirmed. The CancelledError handler (headless_solver.py:491-500) has `if self.deps.confirmed_flag and not self._confirmed:` before returning FLAG_FOUND; the generic handler (501-505) `except Exception as e: ... return self._result(ERROR)` has no equivalent check, and _result() reports flag=self._flag (None). A provider/network error raised inside the same Agent.run after a confirmed submit therefore surfaces ERROR even though the platform accepted the flag. Recovery is possible if a later loop pass returns normally (line 479) but not guaranteed: 3 consecutive errors break (swarm.py:358-364) and a set cancel_event stops further runs. (The cited 'tracer write failure' example cannot actually raise - SolverTracer._write swallows all exceptions at tracing.py:35-40 - but the defect itself stands.)

summary: Operator bump landing mid-run is silently discarded by the `_messages` reassignment in the run loop
detail: `bump()` appends the ModelRequest to `self._messages` (line 556), but a run already in flight captured `message_history=self._messages` (line 453) and will overwrite the list wholesale at line 466 (`self._messages = result.all_messages()`), dropping the appended message — the appended MessageRequest never reaches the live agent run and never survives it. This is the exact path used by the web console's "talk to the agent": coordinator_loop.py:425 calls `solver.bump(...)` on a running solver, so operator guidance is lost with no error and no trace beyond the `bump` event.

summary: Dedup/cooldown/circuit-breaker state is per-swarm-instance and reset by every re-spawn, so the platform error budget is not protected across attempts
detail: All submission bookkeeping (_confirmed_flags/_accepted_flags/_submit_count/_submitted_flags/_last_submit_time/_wrong_total/_submit_locked, swarm.py:96-102) lives on the ChallengeSwarm instance and is serialised only by its own asyncio.Lock — correct within one instance/event loop, but every re-spawn builds a fresh ChallengeSwarm (coordinator_core.py:112-119). The early-exit retry path (coordinator_core.py:121-134) re-queues any challenge whose swarm returned None — precisely what a circuit-breaker stand-down produces — and /resume plus the deadlock auto-resume also respawn (coordinator_loop.py:238-256, 385-392). The breaker resets to 0 wrong submissions and _submitted_flags is empty, so previously rejected flags can be guessed again and the per-task wrong-submission protection does not survive restarts.
fix_hint: Keep per-challenge submission bookkeeping on CoordinatorDeps (keyed by challenge name) and seed each new swarm from it; or refuse auto-retry when the previous attempt ended via circuit_breaker (surface the reason instead of returning None).
evidence: Confirmed. All submission bookkeeping is per-instance (swarm.py:96-102) and every respawn builds a fresh ChallengeSwarm (coordinator_core.py:111-121). The early-retry path (coordinator_core.py:130-147) re-queues a challenge whose swarm returned None - which is what a breaker stand-down produces, since swarm.run returns self.winner (:461-462), None whenever nothing reached FLAG_FOUND - and /resume (coordinator_loop.py:379-386) plus the deadlock auto-resume (:459-461) also respawn. Each fresh swarm starts with _wrong_total=0, _submit_locked=False and an empty _submitted_flags, so previously rejected flags can be guessed again and the breaker does not survive restarts.

summary: resolve_model_settings' max_tokens never reaches the wire as `max_tokens`: pydantic-ai emits it as `max_completion_tokens` for all three providers, and the deepseek cap equals the entire 128k context window.

Installed pydantic-ai maps the setting away from `max_tokens`: `supports_max_completion_tokens = profile.get('openai_chat_supports_max_completion_tokens', True)` -> `max_completion_tokens=max_tokens if supports_max_completion_tokens else OMIT` (pydantic_ai/models/openai.py:1450, 1460-1461); only azure (azure.py:154) and openrouter (openrouter.py:199) flip the flag, and backend/models.py uses a plain OpenAIProvider (L76/102/111/140). Nuance: for qwen's default responses mode it maps to max_output_tokens (openai.py:3254), so 'for all three providers' is slightly overbroad, but the deepseek/glm substance stands.

summary: Child processes escape the guard entirely: only in-process Python sockets are restricted, while subprocess/os.system/ctypes reach any host.
detail: The docstring states 'outbound socket connections from the snippet are restricted to these hosts (target lock) plus localhost', but `subprocess.run(['curl', 'http://10.0.3.9/'])`, `os.system`, `os.popen`, `ctypes` or any bundled binary run outside the interpreter where the monkeypatch has no effect. The tool contract shown to the model (prompts.py:137-138) and the degraded-lock message ('ALL outbound network access is locked', headless_solver.py:401-409) overstate enforcement; a snippet can trivially reproduce the c-03 drift the lock exists to prevent.
fix_hint: State the in-process-only limitation honestly in the tool description/prompt, and/or add OS-level egress control for locked runs (per-child firewall rule, job object, network namespace); pure in-process patching cannot cover this.
evidence: Claim matches the code. The guard rebinds only socket functions inside the snippet's own interpreter (local_exec.py:59-68); nothing intercepts child processes. Docstring at local_exec.py:35-36 claims `outbound socket connections from the snippet are restricted to these hosts (target lock) plus localhost`, and prompts.py:137-138 tells the model `run_python socket connections to any other host are blocked` - but `subprocess.run(['curl', ...])`, os.system/os.popen/ctypes or any child interpreter never execute the preamble, so egress fully escapes the stated guarantee.

summary: asyncio.open_connection bypasses the guard on Windows' default Proactor loop (ConnectEx on the raw fd).
detail: The preamble wraps only `socket.socket.connect` and `socket.create_connection`. On Unix the selector loop calls `sock.connect` (Lib/asyncio/selector_events.py:651) and is caught, but on Windows `loop.create_connection` -> `ProactorEventLoop.sock_connect` (Lib/asyncio/proactor_events.py:724) -> `IocpProactor.connect`, which issues `ov.ConnectEx(conn.fileno(), address)` (Lib/asyncio/windows_events.py:597) directly on the fd and never calls the Python method — and this project runs on win32. `asyncio.run(asyncio.open_connection('10.0.3.9', 80))` inside a snippet therefore reaches any host while the guard believes egress is restricted.
fix_hint: Language-level socket patches cannot intercept ConnectEx: wrap/deny `asyncio.open_connection` and `loop.create_connection` (e.g. replace them with guard-checking versions when sys.platform == 'win32'), or document the platform gap and enforce egress at the OS level (firewall/job object) for locked runs.
evidence: Code matches the claim. local_exec.py:59-68 patches only `_socket.socket.connect = _connect` and `_socket.create_connection`; CPython 3.14 win32 (verified in the local stdlib) makes Proactor the default (`_DefaultEventLoopPolicy = _WindowsProactorEventLoopPolicy`, Lib/asyncio/windows_events.py) and its connect path runs `return await self._proactor.connect(sock, address)` (proactor_events.py:723-724) -> `ov.ConnectEx(conn.fileno(), address)` (windows_events.py:597) directly on the fd, never calling the patched Python method. The Unix selector path does call `sock.connect(address)` (selector_events.py:651) and is caught. So `asyncio.run(asyncio.open_connection('10.0.3.9', 80))` inside a snippet bypasses the target lock on this project's platform.

summary: Guard patches only socket.socket.connect; connect_ex, the _socket.socket base class, and the exposed _orig_connect name all bypass the target lock.
detail: `_socket.socket.connect = _connect` patches the Python subclass (CPython 3.14 Lib/socket.py:218 defines `class socket(_socket.socket)`), leaving three bypasses: (a) `s.connect_ex((host, port))` — a distinct C method on the same class, never wrapped, enough for a one-call TCP bypass (ssl.SSLSocket.connect_ex routes to `super().connect_ex(addr)`, Lib/ssl.py:1389, so TLS too; only `super().connect`, Lib/ssl.py:1392, is caught); (b) `import _socket; _socket.socket(...)` gives the C base class whose connect is untouched; (c) the originals are left as snippet-module globals (`_orig_connect` line 59, `_orig_ce` line 64), so user code can call `_orig_connect(sock, addr)` directly or restore `socket.socket.connect = _orig_connect`. The docstring promises outbound connections 'are restricted to these hosts (target lock) plus localhost' (lines 35-37).
fix_hint: Wrap connect_ex and sendto/sendmsg on both the Python subclass and the C base class, hide the originals via default-arg binding (`def _connect(self, address, _orig=_orig_connect)`) and del the names, and add a snippet-level test that exercises connect/connect_ex/_socket.socket directly.
evidence: backend/tools/local_exec.py preamble lines 51-70: only `_orig_connect = _socket.socket.connect` (59) is replaced (`_socket.socket.connect = _connect`, 63) plus `_orig_ce = _socket.create_connection` (64) / patch (68) / `del _socket` (69). CPython 3.14 Lib/socket.py:218 defines `class socket(_socket.socket)` overriding neither connect nor connect_ex, so `sock.connect_ex((host, port))` reaches the unpatched C method (Lib/_socket) — and ssl.py:1389 SSLSocket.connect_ex calls `super().connect_ex(...)` (only the connect path at 1392 was the concern), so `socket.connect_ex` and SSL connect_ex bypass the guard; `import _socket; _socket.socket(...)` bypasses it too since the patch is applied on the subclass attribute. The guard also does not cover `socket.socketpair`/`sendto` on UDP paths. `_orig_connect`/`_orig_ce` are left as snippet globals (only `_socket` is deleted at 69), so the code can re-invoke the unpatched originals, contradicting the stated sandbox promise in the module docstring (35-37).

summary: tcp_send's read phase has no overall deadline: a slow-drip service stalls the tool call for the rest of the task budget.
detail: `read_timeout` only bounds `asyncio.open_connection` (net_tools.py:105-107); the read loop `while total < MAX_TCP_OUTPUT:` awaits `reader.read(8192)` with `timeout=keep_open_seconds` (118-126) and exits only on 3s of silence, EOF, or 24KB. A service emitting a byte every <3s keeps the loop alive (up to 24,000 reads, i.e. hours at 1 byte/2.9s), and nothing clamps the exchange to the solver's remaining budget — cancellation only arrives when the challenge time limit cancels the run (no wait_for wraps solver.run_until_done_or_gave_up, swarm.py:329). One tool call can therefore consume the whole remaining task time.
fix_hint: Wrap the entire send/read exchange in `asyncio.wait_for(..., timeout=read_timeout)` (or a dedicated max_exchange_seconds) so the stated read timeout is also a hard ceiling, keeping the 3s silence window as the soft end condition.
evidence: Claim matches the code. net_tools.py:105-107 wraps only `asyncio.wait_for(asyncio.open_connection(host, port), timeout=read_timeout)`; the read loop L119-120 (`while total < MAX_TCP_OUTPUT:` / `chunk = await asyncio.wait_for(reader.read(8192), timeout=keep_open_seconds)`) exits only on 3s silence, EOF, or 24KB, so a >1-byte-per-3s drip keeps it alive up to 24,000 reads (hours). Nothing wraps the exchange: swarm.py:329 `result = await solver.run_until_done_or_gave_up()` is unbounded; the only clamp is the challenge wall-clock `asyncio.wait({run_task}, timeout=limit)` (coordinator_core.py:170).

summary: tsec_platform.py — the most logic-dense adapter in the repo — has no test coverage at all.
detail: No test files exist anywhere in the tree (only .venv matches) although pytest>=9.0 and pytest-asyncio are declared dev dependencies (pyproject.toml:30-31). Untested logic includes: base_url joining and non-JSON handling (49-97), 409 max-active backoff (331-354), close retry/4xx semantics (371-401), duplicate and invalid_state mapping incl. multi-flag challenge_complete (194-259), pull polling and `_started_addrs` bookkeeping (410-465), ghost reaping (277-305). Every one of these behaviors is currently validated only against the live platform.
fix_hint: Add tests/test_tsec_platform.py using httpx.MockTransport (fully offline) covering the branches listed; wire it into the planned pytest gate.
evidence: backend/tsec_platform.py has no covering tests (verified: no tests/ dir, no test_*.py/conftest.py outside .venv; pyproject.toml:29-31 only declares pytest/pytest-asyncio). The named untested branches all exist at the cited locations: base_url joining/non-JSON handling 49-97, 409 max-active backoff 331-354, close retry/4xx semantics 371-401, duplicate and invalid_state mapping incl. multi-flag challenge_complete 194-259, pull polling and _started_addrs bookkeeping 410-465, ghost reaping 277-305. Findings 7/8/9/10 are concrete defects that landed exactly in these untested paths.

summary: TLS certificate verification is disabled on the client that carries the BENCHMARK_TOKEN.
detail: `_ensure_client` passes `verify=False` (line 57) while sending the scoring token in the `BENCHMARK_TOKEN` header (lines 62-65), so any host on the network path can transparently intercept or alter start/submit/close traffic and credentials without a certificate error (httpx only emits an InsecureRequestWarning). The adjacent comment justifies `trust_env=False` alone; nothing explains or gates certificate verification, and this client is the transport for an official scoring run.
fix_hint: Default to verify=True; if the endpoint needs a private/self-signed CA, make it an explicit opt-in setting with a bundled CA and log a warning when disabled.
evidence: backend/tsec_platform.py:55-65: `async with httpx.AsyncClient(..., verify=False) as client:` with `headers = {... "BENCHMARK_TOKEN": self.token}` — TLS certificate verification is disabled with no opt-in setting, allowlist, or warning while the benchmark API token is sent on every request; the only other verify=False is net_tools.py:59. MITM/tamper risk on the office network the user explicitly described. (No network was used in this verification.)

summary: Multi-flag duplicate submissions can never report challenge_complete, even when every flag is already banked.
detail: The duplicate branch (lines 208-227) decides purely from the local `flag_count`: every multi-flag duplicate returns challenge_complete=False with "Other flags are still open" (213-221), never consults the platform completion evidence already present in the cached stub (`is_completed`/`correct_flag_count`, normalized at 142-152), and never updates `_solved_cache` (contrast the success path at 245). If a fully-solved multi-flag challenge receives a duplicate — reachable when an operator /resume re-spawns a deferred challenge that was solved meanwhile (coordinator_loop.py:381-385 routes through `_auto_spawn_one`, which never checks known_solved) — the swarm is told "partial credit" on every submission and can burn its full wall-clock budget, because the poller has no solved transition left to kill it; swarm.py:260 trusts challenge_complete for its confirm logic.
fix_hint: On duplicate, refresh/consult the platform record (is_completed, or correct_flag_count >= flag_count, or counts in the error body) and set challenge_complete plus `_solved_cache.add(...)` when complete.
evidence: backend/tsec_platform.py:208-227 duplicate branch: for multi-flag challenges it always returns `SubmitResult(..., challenge_complete=False)` (lines 213-221) — the cached platform evidence `ch.get('is_completed')` / `ch.get('correct_flag_count')` (lines 137-138, 148-149) is never consulted, and `self._solved_cache.add(name)` runs only in the correct path (line 245). swarm.py:260 `if result.challenge_complete or not multi_flag:` therefore treats an already-complete challenge as still in progress, sending solvers back to hunt for flags that no longer exist until budget exhaustion. Trigger: operator /resume of a challenge solved out-of-band; the duplicate answer's 'already solved' status is returned with challenge_complete=False.

summary: Platform-state submit errors (invalid_state, unknown challenge, generic API errors) map to status "unknown", which the swarm counts as a wrong guess.
detail: `invalid_state` (lines 228-233) and every other non-duplicate error (line 234) — plus the challenge-not-found path at 187-191 — return status "unknown", indistinguishable from a genuinely wrong flag. swarm.py increments `_submit_count`/`_wrong_total` for any status that is neither "correct" nor "already_solved" (swarm.py:273-275), driving escalating cooldowns (swarm.py:227-238) and the four-strike circuit breaker (swarm.py:276-291). Consequence: submissions rejected while the platform is mid-close/mid-start, or a transient failure of the challenge-list refetch, can trip "SUBMIT LOCKED ... incorrect submissions" without a single wrong guess and stand the swarm down early.
fix_hint: Introduce a distinct status (e.g. "error"/"invalid_state") for platform-state failures and exclude it from the swarm's wrong-count/cooldown accounting.
evidence: backend/tsec_platform.py:228-234 maps invalid_state and other 4xx errors to `SubmitResult(status='unknown', ...)` (also the not-found branch at 187-191). In swarm.py:249-292 try_submit_flag, everything that is not 'correct'/'already_solved' falls through to lines 273-275 `self._submit_count[...] += 1; self._wrong_total += 1`, so infrastructure errors count as wrong submissions — triggering the per-model cooldown (lines 227-238) and, after four (4-strike breaker lines 276-291), the task-wide lock that prompts.py:171 warns about. 'unknown' also fails to distinguish a resubmit-duplicate from a genuinely wrong flag.

summary: A /start that yields no address is never recorded, so an aborted spawn re-POSTs /start on retry and creates a duplicate range instance.
detail: `_started_addrs` gets an entry only when the start response already carries addrs (lines 355-357); the common "container still provisioning" case records nothing. If the 10-poll wait (435-454) times out or every poll request fails, pull_challenge raises (458-465) and the scheduler retries later; since no entry exists, the retry falls into the start branch and POSTs /start again (424-431) while the first instance may still be coming up — exactly the duplicate-instance hazard the code warns about at 424-427 and the README states as a contract ("同一题在进程内只 start 一次", README.md:42). Each duplicate consumes one of the scarce "max active" slots.
fix_hint: Record that a start was issued (sentinel or empty-addr marker) before polling, and make the retry path poll the challenge listing instead of re-POSTing /start.
evidence: backend/tsec_platform.py:355-357: `addrs = ... ; if addrs: self._started_addrs[unique_code] = addrs` — the in-process dedup cache is recorded only when the /start response carries addresses. If provisioning exceeds the pull budget, pull_challenge raises (lines 458-465 `raise`) and the retry path re-POSTs /start without the cache entry (lines 422-434), violating the README.md:42 contract '同一题在进程内只 start 一次（地址缓存复用）' and creating a second platform container instance for the same challenge.

summary: A close rejected with 4xx (e.g. invalid_state "already closed") is reported as failure, permanently leaking a local concurrency slot.
detail: close_challenge re-raises every sub-500 response as terminal (lines 378-381) even though the code's own comment names "invalid_state: already closed" as the expected benign outcome. The caller cannot distinguish "already closed" from "close failed": `_started_addrs` is popped only on success (line 397) and release_challenge returns False (lines 316-322), which coordinator_core.py:211-217 reads as "the container still occupies a platform slot" and keeps counting forever (discard happens only when released is not False). Reachable whenever a close succeeded server-side but the client saw a 5xx/timeout and retried into a 4xx — the exact sequence the retry loop at 371-394 produces — and each occurrence shrinks the local concurrency window; repeated occurrences wedge the scheduler at "At capacity" while platform slots are actually free.
fix_hint: Parse the 4xx body: treat invalid_state/'already closed' as success (pop `_started_addrs`, let release_challenge return True), or return a tri-state so the coordinator can reconcile.
evidence: backend/tsec_platform.py:378-381: `except httpx.HTTPStatusError as e: # 4xx (e.g. invalid_state: already closed) is a terminal answer. / if e.response.status_code < 500: raise` — the comment says the request is already terminal, but the code aborts the retry loop by raising, and `_started_addrs.pop(unique_code, None)` is only reached after the loop (line 397). A transient 4xx therefore leaks the address-cache entry forever (README.md:42 '容器防重' contract broken), and release_challenge (307-322) swallows exceptions into `return False`, which routes the challenge into coordinator_core.py:211-217's permanent slot leak ('keeping it counted').

summary: Runtime dependencies are unpinned and uv.lock is gitignored, so upstream builds are not reproducible for a version-sensitive dependency set.
detail: All runtime deps are bare names: pydantic-ai[openai], pydantic-settings, genai-prices, httpx, pyyaml, rich, click, fastapi, uvicorn[standard] (pyproject.toml:6-16); .gitignore:26 excludes `uv.lock` even though the worktree contains one (329 KB, present on disk), so fresh clones/CI resolve whatever is current. This audit found behavior that hinges on exact versions: genai-prices provider ids differ per snapshot ('zai'/'zhipuai' in the installed 0.1.11) and pydantic-ai's profile defaults drive the max_tokens/max_completion_tokens mapping (models/openai.py:1450).
fix_hint: Either commit uv.lock (remove .gitignore:26) or add floors/ceilings for the API-sensitive packages, e.g. pydantic-ai>=2.56,<3, genai-prices>=0.1.11,<0.2, openai>=3.30,<4.
evidence: Claim matches the repo state. pyproject.toml:6-16 lists bare names (`"pydantic-ai[openai]", "pydantic-settings", "genai-prices", ...`) and .gitignore:26 is `uv.lock` (git check-ignore -v reports `.gitignore:26:uv.lock`, and the file is untracked) although a 329 KB uv.lock exists on disk. Repro risk is concrete: behavior here depends on exact snapshots (genai-prices provider ids; pydantic-ai `profile.get('openai_chat_supports_max_completion_tokens', True)`, pydantic_ai/models/openai.py:1450).

summary: The trace analyzer parses events the solver no longer emits and ignores the current telemetry, leaving one failure class unreachable and the new steering signals invisible.
detail: It still parses `no_progress_warning` and `loop_break` (scripts/analyze_traces.py:242-245) and documents them in the schema comment (L16, L20-21), but the rewritten solver never emits them (docs/rewrite-plan.md removes no-progress steering; current events are emitted at backend/agents/headless_solver.py:162/185/395/436/534/558/587 and backend/agents/tracing_toolset.py:45/55/65). Consequently failure rule 4 `gave_up_stalled` (L320-321) can never fire, yet the report prints its description (L491-492) and a per-class count that is permanently 0. Conversely, `loop_detected` (tracing_toolset.py:45), `target_lock_degraded` (headless_solver.py:395) and `findings_injected` (tracing_toolset.py:65) are not parsed at all, and counters that are incremented — bumps, flag_confirm_events, target_lock_blocks, loop_breaks (L123, L134-137, L224, L241-247) — are never printed, so the report silently lacks the run's actual steering telemetry.
fix_hint: Delete the stale branches/rules/docstring lines, parse and report loop_detected/target_lock_degraded/findings_injected (and print the already-collected counters), or drop counters that are never reported.
evidence: Claim matches the code. analyze_traces.py:242-245 still parses `no_progress_warning` / `loop_break` (documented L20-21), but no backend file emits them (grep over backend/ finds no such tracer events), so rule 4 at L320-321 (`elif r.final_status == "gave_up" and r.no_progress_warnings:`) can never fire while its description is still printed (L491-492). Conversely `loop_detected` (tracing_toolset.py:45), `target_lock_degraded` (headless_solver.py:395-400) and `findings_injected` (tracing_toolset.py:65) are emitted but never parsed, and the counters bumps/flag_confirm_events/target_lock_blocks/loop_breaks (L123-137, 224, 241-247) are never emitted into the report.

summary: The interactive REPL's `input()` runs in the default executor and cannot be cancelled, so the process can hang at exit after /quit or Ctrl+C.
detail: `line = await loop.run_in_executor(None, input, "> ")` — cancelling `repl_task` in the shutdown finally (lines 308-314) cancels the awaiting future but leaves the worker thread blocked inside `input()`. `asyncio.run()` finishes with `loop.shutdown_default_executor()`, which joins default-executor worker threads (and `concurrent.futures`' atexit hook joins them too), so in `-i` mode the interpreter can block at exit until the operator presses Enter; on Windows (the target platform) a detached or closed console makes this look like a hard hang after the scheduler has already logged 'Scheduler shutting down...'.
fix_hint: Read stdin on a dedicated daemon thread that pushes lines into `operator_inbox` (the thread dies with the process), or accept lines only when `sys.stdin.isatty()` and fall back to non-interactive; do not depend on cancelling a future parked in `input()`.

summary: The `max(1, ...)` clamp on `challenge_time_limit_seconds` is stored on a `CoordinatorDeps` field that nothing reads; the time-limit consumer reads raw settings, so `--time-limit 0` kills every swarm instantly.
detail: `build_deps` writes `challenge_time_limit_seconds=max(1, getattr(settings, 'challenge_time_limit_seconds', 1800))` into deps, but no code reads `deps.challenge_time_limit_seconds` (verified by grep); `_time_limit_for_challenge` reads `int(getattr(settings, 'challenge_time_limit_seconds', 1800))` directly (swarm.py:60), and `--time-limit` is declared `type=int` with no lower bound (cli.py:91). `--time-limit 0` or a negative value therefore produces `limit = 0` when no total budget is set: `asyncio.wait({run_task}, timeout=0)` returns before the swarm runs, `swarm.kill('wall_clock')` fires, and every challenge is deferred with 'time limit reached (0s)', while `_create_solver` still hands solvers `max(300, 0 - 60) = 300` seconds. In the budget-tracked path the clamp expression `max(60, min(limit, int(remaining_global_seconds)))` can likewise exceed the remaining global budget whenever `min_remaining_seconds_to_spawn` is configured below 60.
fix_hint: Pass the clamped deps value into `_time_limit_for_challenge` (or clamp at the use site with `max(60, ...)`), add `click.IntRange(min=60)` to `--time-limit`, and either delete the dead deps field or make it the single source of truth.

summary: One malformed or truncated `metadata.yml` aborts `build_deps`, so a previously crashed run can brick every subsequent startup.
detail: The scan loop calls `ChallengeMeta.from_yaml(meta_path)` with no error handling (lines 129-135). `from_yaml` performs `yaml.safe_load` plus conversions such as `int(data.get('flag_count', 1) or 1)` (prompts.py:47-56), which raise on truncated YAML or non-numeric fields; `pull_challenge` writes that file with a plain `write_text` (tsec_platform.py:481-484), so a run killed mid-write leaves a partial file that makes the next `ctf-solve` invocation crash before the event loop starts, with no way to skip the bad directory.
fix_hint: Wrap the per-directory parse in try/except, log a warning and skip (or re-pull) the offending directory, and write metadata.yml via a temp file plus os.replace to make it crash-safe.

summary: `__bump__` target lookups sit outside the guarded parse, so an unhashable JSON value raises TypeError and aborts the entire run as 'Scheduler fatal'.
detail: The try/except (lines 410-417) covers only `json.loads` and the two subscripts; `swarm = deps.swarms.get(challenge)` (line 420) and `solver = swarm.solvers.get(model)` (line 421) run unguarded. A payload such as `{"challenge": ["x"], "model": "y", "message": "hi"}` parses cleanly and then raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'`; it escapes the operator drain loop into `except Exception as e: logger.error("Scheduler fatal: %s", e, exc_info=True)` (lines 305-306), so one malformed console/websocket message (web.py serializes whatever the UI sends, lines 237-243) terminates the benchmark run, which is then reported to the CLI as a normal return with no error status. Relatedly, `solver.bump(...)` is applied even when the solver's run has already finished (entries in `swarm.solvers` are never removed), so the guidance is dropped while `logger.info('Operator bumped ...')` (line 426) claims delivery.
fix_hint: Validate/coerce before the lookups (`challenge = str(data['challenge'])`, `model = str(data['model'])`) or move the lookups inside the try and add TypeError/AttributeError to it; check swarm/solver liveness before reporting the bump as delivered.

summary: Flag extraction/normalization/rescue and target-lock helpers have zero tests
detail: `_extract_flag_candidates` (51-58), `_norm_flag_text` (61-63), `_flag_inner` (66-70), `_is_rejected_variant` (73-84), `_parse_allowed_hosts` (87-98) and `_target_lock_block` (101-134) are pure, safety-critical functions — they decide what gets submitted and what gets blocked — yet the repo contains no tests at all (no `tests/` directory and no `test_*.py` outside .venv). The bugs above (IPv6 parsing, case-folded suppression, rescue breadth) are exactly what table-driven unit tests would catch.
fix_hint: Add pytest coverage: IPv6/bracketed/ported hosts, rejected-variant edge cases (case, prefix swaps, whitespace), rescue extraction from mixed prose, and lock allow/deny for http_request/tcp_send.

summary: Case-folding reject-variant suppression can drop a distinct, possibly correct flag
detail: `_norm_flag_text` lowercases and strips whitespace (61-63) and `_is_rejected_variant` compares normalized text (line 79) as well as inner content across different prefixes (82-83). Flags are compared exactly by the platform (tsec_platform sends `flag.strip()` verbatim and defines no `normalize_flag`), so a candidate `flag{AbC}` is treated as "already rejected" after `flag{abc}` failed, even though the platform never judged the exact string — the rescue path silently skips it. The inner-content rule likewise conflates `CTF{x}` and `flag{x}`.
fix_hint: Compare exact strings for the already-rejected check (keep the inner-content heuristic only for same-case re-wrapped decoys), or centralize normalization in a platform-level `normalize_flag` hook that reflects the platform's actual case rules.

summary: Allowed-host parsing mangles IPv6 targets, silently locking the whole task
detail: `part = re.sub(r"^https?://", "", part).strip("[]").split("/")[0]` followed by `host = part.rsplit(":", 1)[0] if ":" in part else part` (94-95) assumes the last colon is a port separator: for `[2001:db8::1]:8080` the extracted "host" is `2001:db8::1]` (only the leading bracket is stripped and the trailing bracket survives), and for a bare `2001:db8::1` it is `2001:db8:`. Every request/tcp_send to the real target then fails the exact-match check at 126 ("is not one of your assigned targets") while `allowed_hosts` is non-empty, so the degraded-mode warning never fires — the solver is silently locked out of its own target.
fix_hint: Parse with `urllib.parse.urlsplit` / a helper that strips brackets before splitting on ":", or detect IPv6 literals with `ipaddress` and compare normalized addresses.

summary: _parse_allowed_hosts mis-parses bracketed/IPv6 targets, so the real target never enters the allow set and all its requests are blocked.
detail: `.strip("[]")` runs before the port split and `rsplit(":", 1)` assumes IPv4: `[2001:db8::1]:8443` -> `2001:db8::1]`; `[10.0.1.5]:80` -> `10.0.1.5]`; bare `2001:db8::1` -> `2001:db8:`. The resulting junk strings are added to the allow set (line 97) while the actual hostname `2001:db8::1` is absent, so `http_request('http://[2001:db8::1]:8443/')` (urlparse hostname `2001:db8::1`) and run_python connections to it are both falsely BLOCKED; the task becomes unsolvable with no useful diagnostic. Duplicate/case handling is otherwise fine (set + lower()).
fix_hint: Parse with `urlsplit("//" + part)` or handle brackets explicitly: if part starts with '[' and contains ']', take the bracketed host and ignore the rest; else only rsplit the port when the part has exactly one ':'. Add a table-driven test for ip:port, url:port/path, [v6]:port, bare v6, duplicates and case.
evidence: Code matches the claim: headless_solver.py:94 `part = re.sub(r"^https?://", "", part).strip("[]").split("/")[0]` and L95 `host = part.rsplit(":", 1)[0] if ":" in part else part` turn `[2001:db8::1]:8443` into `2001:db8::1]`, `[10.0.1.5]:80` into `10.0.1.5]`, and bare `2001:db8::1` into `2001:db8:`; L97 adds the junk to the set while the real hostname (urlparse hostname `2001:db8::1`) is absent, so _target_lock_block (L125-127) blocks the assigned target. Real parse defect, but TSecBench targets are IPv4 VPN addresses (10.0.x.x per prompts.py/net_tools.py) so the bracketed/IPv6 form does not occur in practice - latent, corrected to low.

summary: `last_progress_step` is written in three places and never read — leftover of the deleted hint stall gate

No code in backend/ reads the field after construction; `request_hint` is gated only by `hint_used`. Dead state plus comments that misdescribe current behavior.

summary: `scenario` plumbing in the solver is inert, and the module docstring misstates the target lock's basis

The prompts.py module docstring (line 7) claims `_guess_scenario` is used "to pick a per-challenge time budget and to gate the target lock" — the lock claim is false; the function's own docstring (prompts.py:65) says the opposite: "never affects the target lock, which is purely structural".

detail: Repo-wide grep (excluding .venv): `scenario=_guess_scenario(meta)` is stored on deps (deps.py:54) and read nowhere; `use_vision` is set at 344/350 (deps.py:29) and read nowhere; `last_progress_step` is written at 239, 297, 532 with comments calling it progress 'for the hint stall gate' although request_hint now says 'there is no gate' (255-259). `resume_context` (constructor param 328, used at 411-412 to append text to the system prompt) is a leftover of the deleted checkpoint/resume subsystem (rewrite-plan §6) and is always empty in the only production call site (swarm.py:148).
